title: Chapter 8 — Pelecaniformes
description: A diverse order of waterbirds that includes herons, egrets, bitterns, pelicans, ibises, and spoonbills. Herons and bitterns (Ardeidae) are the most widespread and familiar group, found on every continent except Antarctica. They are characterised by long legs, long necks, and dagger-like bills used to strike fish and amphibians with lightning speed.

children.name: Ardea
children.description: Great herons and egrets — the largest and most familiar members of the family. The grey heron (gråhäger) is one of the most recognisable birds in Sweden: a tall, slate-grey sentinel standing motionless at the water's edge for hours, then striking with lightning speed to impale a fish with its dagger bill. Grey herons nest colonially in tall trees ('heronries') — colonies in Swedish parks and forests can be centuries old and contain hundreds of pairs. The great white egret (ägretthäger) was once so rare in Sweden that a sighting was a national event; following a dramatic European range expansion it now breeds in southern Swedish marshes and is increasingly common as a winter visitor in Stockholm.

children.name: Ardea cinerea
children.description: The grey heron is a long-legged wading bird of the heron family, Ardeidae, native throughout temperate Europe and Asia, and also parts of Africa. It is resident in much of its range, but some populations from the more northern parts migrate southwards in autumn. A bird of wetland areas, it can be seen around lakes, rivers, ponds, marshes and on the sea coast.

children.name: Ardea alba
children.description: The great egret, also known as the common egret, large egret, great white egret, or great white heron, is a large, widely distributed egret. The four subspecies are found in Asia, Africa, the Americas, and southern Europe. Recently, it has also been spreading to more northern areas of Europe.

children.name: Ardea purpurea
children.description: The purple heron (Ardea purpurea) is a wide-ranging heron species.

children.name: Ardea herodias
children.description: The great blue heron is a large wading bird in the heron family (Ardeidae), common near shores of open water and wetlands over most of North and Central America, as well as Northwestern South America, the Caribbean, and the Galápagos Islands. It is occasionally found in the Azores and is a rare vagrant to Europe. An all-white population found in South Florida and the Florida Keys is known as the great white heron.

children.name: Ardea cocoi
children.description: The cocoi heron (Ardea cocoi) is a species of long-legged wading bird in the heron family Ardeidae found across South America.

children.name: Ardea intermedia
children.description: The medium egret (Ardea intermedia), median egret, smaller egret or intermediate egret, is a medium-sized heron.

children.name: Ardea goliath
children.description: The Goliath heron (Ardea goliath), also known as the giant heron, is a very large wading bird of the heron family, Ardeidae.

children.name: Bubulcus
children.description: Cattle egrets — stocky white herons that have achieved one of the most remarkable natural range expansions in ornithological history. Originally confined to Africa and southern Asia, cattle egrets colonised South America by the early 20th century, spread through the Americas to North America by the 1950s, and have since established themselves on every inhabited continent. They follow large grazing animals — or tractors and lawn mowers — to catch invertebrates flushed by their movements.

children.name: Butorides
children.description: Striated herons and their allies — small, compact herons with dark, streaked plumage that inhabit dense vegetation along waterways worldwide. These are among the most widespread herons, with representatives on every continent except Antarctica. They are famously resourceful hunters, occasionally using bait — dropping feathers, insects, or bread onto water — to lure fish within striking range, one of very few documented tool-use behaviours in birds.

children.name: Butorides striata
children.description: The striated heron (Butorides striata) also known as mangrove heron or little green heron, is a small heron, about 44 cm tall.

children.name: Butorides virescens
children.description: The green heron is a small heron of North and Central America. Butorides is from Middle English butor "bittern" and Ancient Greek -oides, "resembling", and virescens is Latin for "greenish".

children.name: Butorides sundevalli
children.description: | range_map = Butorides sundevalli map.svg.

children.name: Ardeola
children.description: Pond herons — small, squat herons of the Old World tropics, notable for their cryptic brown streaked plumage when at rest and their startlingly white wings revealed in flight. Six species divide the tropical Old World from West Africa through Madagascar and South Asia to Southeast Asia. They are birds of rice paddies, marshes, and vegetated pond margins, where their mottled resting plumage makes them nearly invisible until they take wing.

children.name: Ardeola ralloides
children.description: The squacco heron (Ardeola ralloides) is a small heron, long, of which the body is , with wingspan.

children.name: Ardeola grayii
children.description: The Indian pond heron or paddybird (Ardeola grayii) is a small heron.

children.name: Ardeola bacchus
children.description: The Chinese pond heron (Ardeola bacchus) is an East Asian freshwater bird of the heron family, (Ardeidae).

children.name: Egretta
children.description: Typical egrets and reef herons — a diverse genus of mostly small to medium white or dark herons found on every continent. The genus spans all habitats from mountain streams to coral reefs, and includes species with both white and dark colour morphs. Several were decimated by the 19th-century plume trade, which drove demand for their elaborate breeding aigrettes used in women's hats; their recovery sparked the founding of the Audubon Society and early conservation movements.

children.name: Egretta garzetta
children.description: The little egret (Egretta garzetta) is a species of small heron in the family Ardeidae.

children.name: Egretta thula
children.description: The snowy egret is the American counterpart to the very similar Old World little egret, which has become established in the Bahamas.

children.name: Egretta eulophotes
children.description: The Chinese egret or Swinhoe's egret (Egretta eulophotes) is a threatened species of egret from east Asia, first described by Robert Swinhoe in 1860.

children.name: Egretta vinaceigula
children.description: The slaty egret (Egretta vinaceigula) is a small, dark egret found in southern Africa.

children.name: Egretta picata
children.description: The pied heron (Egretta picata), also known as the pied egret is a bird found in coastal and subcoastal areas of monsoonal northern Australia as well as some parts of Wallacea and New Guinea.

children.name: Egretta sacra
children.description: The Pacific reef heron (Egretta sacra), also known as the eastern reef heron or eastern reef egret, is a species of heron found throughout southern Asia and Oceania.

children.name: Egretta rufescens
children.description: The reddish egret (Egretta rufescens) is a medium-sized heron that is a resident breeder in Central America, the Bahamas, the Caribbean, the Gulf Coast of the United States (primarily Texas), and Mexico.

children.name: Egretta caerulea
children.description: The little blue heron (Egretta caerulea) is a small heron of the genus Egretta.

children.name: Egretta tricolor
children.description: The tricolored heron (Egretta tricolor), formerly known as the Louisiana heron, is a small species of heron native to coastal parts of the Americas.

children.name: Egretta gularis
children.description: The western reef heron (Egretta gularis), also called the western reef egret, is a medium-sized heron found in southern Europe, Africa and parts of Asia.

children.name: Egretta dimorpha
children.description: thumb|white and black morph together The dimorphic egret (Egretta dimorpha) is a species of heron in the family Ardeidae.

children.name: Egretta ardesiaca
children.description: The black heron (Egretta ardesiaca), also known as the black egret, is an African heron.

children.name: Agamia
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the spectacular Agami Heron of Central and South American rainforest streams. It is among the most brilliantly coloured of all herons, with iridescent green, chestnut, and silver plumage, and a remarkably long, slender bill adapted for hunting small fish in fast-flowing, shaded forest streams.

children.name: Agamia agami
children.description: The agami heron (Agamia agami) is a medium-sized heron.

children.name: Pilherodius
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Capped Heron, a medium-sized, strikingly patterned heron of South American river margins. It bears a unique combination of a black cap, white or creamy-buff body, and a long blue facial lore, unlike any other heron in its range.

children.name: Pilherodius pileatus
children.description: thumb|Pilherodius pileatus Río Amacayacu, Amazonas, Colombia The capped heron (Pilherodius pileatus) is a water bird endemic to the neotropics, inhabiting rainforest from the center of Panama to the south of Brazil.

children.name: Cochlearius
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Boat-billed Heron — a distinctive, nocturnal heron of Neotropical mangroves and forest waterways whose enormous, boat-shaped bill is unique among all wading birds. The bill is thought to be adapted for scooping prey from soft mud or shallow water in low-light conditions.

children.name: Tigrisoma
children.description: Tiger-herons — large, heavily barred or streaked herons of tropical American forest rivers and streams. The intricate tiger-striped pattern provides superb camouflage in dappled forest light. They are among the most handsome herons in the world, with rich rufous, black, and buff markings, and inhabit the banks of fast-flowing lowland and foothill rivers.

children.name: Tigrisoma salmoni
children.description: A very poorly known tiger-heron restricted to the Pacific slope of Colombia and possibly northwestern Ecuador, inhabiting dense forest streams and swamp-forest edges. Named after the 19th-century British collector Thomas Salmon who collected specimens in Colombia. Sometimes treated as a subspecies of the Rufescent Tiger-Heron.

children.name: Tigriornis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the White-crested Tiger-Heron, an enigmatic and little-studied forest heron of West and Central African rainforest rivers. Distinguished from the American tiger-herons by its white crest and confined to the humid lowland forests of the Congo Basin and West African rainforest belt.

children.name: Zebrilus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Zigzag Heron, the smallest of the tiger-pattern herons and one of the least-known birds in the world. Restricted to Amazonian forest streams in South America, it is so secretive and rare in collections that little is known of its behaviour or ecology.

children.name: Zebrilus undulatus
children.description: The zigzag heron (Zebrilus undulatus) is a species of heron in the family Ardeidae, also including egrets and bitterns.

children.name: Ixobrychus
children.description: Little bitterns — the smallest herons, barely larger than a blackbird. The little bittern (dvärghäger) is a scarce and elusive breeding species in the southernmost Swedish reedlands. Like its larger relative, it freezes with bill pointing skyward when disturbed, relying on its cryptic streaked plumage to disappear among reed stems. Males have black backs and wings with large buff wing patches that flash conspicuously in flight. Little bitterns are nocturnal hunters, creeping through dense reed stems to catch small fish, frogs, and invertebrates. Their call — a soft, rhythmic 'wup-wup-wup' — is one of the quieter and more easily overlooked sounds of a Swedish reedbed.

children.name: Ixobrychus minutus
children.description: The little bittern (Botaurus minutus) is a wading bird in the heron family, Ardeidae.

children.name: Ixobrychus sinensis
children.description: The yellow bittern (Botaurus sinensis) is a small bittern of Old World origins that breeds in the northern Indian subcontinent, east to the Russian Far East, Japan, and Indonesia.

children.name: Ixobrychus cinnamomeus
children.description: The cinnamon bittern (Botaurus cinnamomeus) or chestnut bittern is a small Old World bittern, breeding in tropical and subtropical Asia from India east to China and Indonesia.

children.name: Ixobrychus sturmii
children.description: The dwarf bittern (Botaurus sturmii) is a species of heron in the family Ardeidae that is widely distributed across Sub-Saharan Africa avoiding only the very arid regions.

children.name: Ixobrychus exilis
children.description: The least bittern (Botaurus exilis) is a small heron, the smallest member of the family Ardeidae found in the Americas.

children.name: Ixobrychus flavicollis
children.description: The black bittern (Botaurus flavicollis) is a bittern of Old World origin, breeding in tropical Asia from Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka east to China, Indonesia, and Australia.

children.name: Ixobrychus payesii
children.description: A small, dark bittern of West and Central African forest zones with dark grey upperparts and rufous underparts streaked white, inhabiting the dense margins of forest streams, swamp-forest, and papyrus wetlands. Named after the French naturalist Ernest Payé. Rarely observed and poorly known, with most records from forest-edge habitats during the rains.

children.name: Ixobrychus seychellarum
children.description: A Critically Endangered little bittern endemic to the Seychelles Islands, where the last confirmed sightings were made in the 1940s and the species is likely extinct. It inhabited freshwater marshes and streams on the main granite islands. Its extinction was caused by wetland drainage and the introduction of predatory mammals.

children.name: Botaurus
children.description: Bitterns — cryptically camouflaged, reedbed-dwelling herons with one of the most extraordinary vocalisations in the animal kingdom. The great bittern's 'boom' — a deep, resonant foghorn-like sound carrying up to 5 km — is produced by inflating specialised air sacs in the oesophagus and is most often heard at dawn and dusk in early spring. Bitterns are masters of camouflage: their brown, streaked plumage matches reedbeds perfectly, and when alarmed they stretch upward with bill pointing skyward, swaying gently to mimic reeds in the wind. The Swedish rördrom is a thinly distributed and declining breeding bird, requiring extensive reedlands that are being lost to drainage and water level management.

children.name: Botaurus stellaris
children.description: The Eurasian bittern or great bittern is a wading bird in the bittern subfamily (Botaurinae) of the heron family Ardeidae. There are two subspecies, the northern race breeding in parts of Europe and across the Palearctic, as well as on the northern coast of Africa, while the southern race is endemic to parts of southern Africa. It is a secretive bird, seldom seen in the open as it prefers to skulk in reed beds and thick vegetation near water bodies.

children.name: Botaurus lentiginosus
children.description: The American bittern (Botaurus lentiginosus) is a species of wading bird in the heron family.

children.name: Botaurus pinnatus
children.description: The pinnated bittern (Botaurus pinnatus), also known as the South American bittern, is a large member of the heron family (Ardeidae) found in the New World tropics.

children.name: Botaurus poiciloptilus
children.description: The Australasian bittern (Botaurus poiciloptilus), or in Māori, is a stocky, sizeable and elusive heron-like bird native to the wetlands of Australia, New Zealand, and New Caledonia.

children.name: Syrigma
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Whistling Heron, a slender, pale heron of South American open grasslands and cerrado that is unique in the family for preferring dry savanna habitats well away from water. Its melodious whistling call — unusual among herons — gives it its common name.

children.name: Syrigma sibilatrix
children.description: The whistling heron (Syrigma sibilatrix) is a medium-sized, often terrestrial heron of South America.

children.name: Nycticorax
children.description: Night herons — stocky, large-headed herons active primarily at dusk and night. The Black-crowned Night Heron is one of the world's most widespread herons, nesting colonially on every continent except Australia and Antarctica. Its evocative 'quock' call, delivered in flight at dusk, is a classic sound of evening wetlands across the Northern Hemisphere. Night herons roost in dense vegetation by day and begin hunting fish, frogs, and invertebrates as darkness falls.

children.name: Nycticorax nycticorax
children.description: The black-crowned night heron or black-capped night heron, commonly shortened to just night heron in Eurasia, is a medium-sized heron found throughout a large part of the world, including parts of Europe, Asia, and North and South America. In Australasia it is replaced by the closely related Nankeen night heron, with which it has hybridised in the area of contact.

children.name: Nyctanassa
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Yellow-crowned Night Heron of the Americas, closely related to Nycticorax but distinguished by its striking black-and-white head pattern with a yellow crown, and its specialisation on crustaceans — particularly crabs and crayfish — rather than fish.

children.name: Gorsachius
children.description: Forest night herons — four secretive, heavy-bodied night herons of Asian and African forest zones. These are among the least-known herons in the world, inhabiting dense forest streams and mountain ravines where they are rarely observed. Several species were described from very few specimens and have not been reliably observed in the wild for decades.

children.name: Zonerodius
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Forest Bittern of New Guinea — an enigmatic, very poorly known heron with tiger-like barring that inhabits lowland and foothill forest streams in New Guinea. Rarely collected and seldom observed, it remains one of the least-studied herons in the world.

children.name: Zonerodius heliosylus
children.description: The forest bittern (Zonerodius heliosylus) is a bird indigenous to New Guinea.

children.name: Platalea
children.description: Unmistakeable white or pink waterbirds with spatula-shaped bills swept through shallow water. The Eurasian Spoonbill has colonised the Netherlands and Belgium and is now annual in southern Sweden; breeding is expected.

children.name: Platalea leucorodia
children.description: The Eurasian spoonbill (Platalea leucorodia), or common spoonbill, is a wading bird of the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae, native to Europe, Africa and Asia.

children.name: Platalea regia
children.description: The royal spoonbill (Platalea regia), also known as the black-billed spoonbill lives in intertidal flats and shallows of fresh and saltwater wetlands in Australia, New Zealand, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and the Solomon Islands.

children.name: Platalea alba
children.description: The African spoonbill (Platalea alba) is a long-legged wading bird of the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Platalea ajaja
children.description: The roseate spoonbill (Platalea ajaja) is a social wading bird of the ibis and spoonbill family, Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Plegadis
children.description: Dark, glossy waders with long decurved bills, expanding northward across Europe and the Americas. Their plumage glows with metallic iridescence in direct sunlight.

children.name: Plegadis falcinellus
children.description: The glossy ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) is a water bird in the order Pelecaniformes and the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Plegadis chihi
children.description: The white-faced ibis is a wading bird in the ibis family, Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Plegadis ridgwayi
children.description: The puna ibis (Plegadis ridgwayi) is a species of waterbird in the family Threskiornithidae, spoonbills and ibises.

children.name: Threskiornis
children.description: The sacred ibises — white-plumaged ibises with naked black heads and necks, found across the Old World tropics. The African Sacred Ibis was revered in ancient Egypt as the embodiment of Thoth, the god of writing and wisdom, and was mummified in vast numbers at sites such as Saqqara.

children.name: Threskiornis aethiopicus
children.description: thumb|Observations of African sacred ibis 2015–2022.

children.name: Threskiornis moluccus
children.description: The Australian white ibis (Threskiornis molucca) is a wading bird of the family Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Pseudibis
children.description: Two large, dark ibises of South and Southeast Asian lowlands, distinguished by their bare facial skin and white patches on the shoulders. They are among the most threatened ibises due to extensive habitat loss across their ranges.

children.name: Pseudibis gigantea
children.description: The giant ibis (Pseudibis gigantea) is a wading bird of the ibis family, Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Geronticus
children.description: Two species of bald ibis with completely bare, featherless heads — in contrast to other ibises which have featherless areas only on the face. They nest on cliff ledges rather than in trees. The Northern Bald Ibis was once widespread across Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa; its disappearance from Europe is one of the best-documented avian extinctions on the continent.

children.name: Geronticus eremita
children.description: The northern bald ibis, hermit ibis, or Waldrapp (Geronticus eremita) is a migratory Old World ibis found in open areas such as grasslands, rocky mountains, and semi-deserts, often close to running water.

children.name: Nipponia
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Crested Ibis — one of the rarest birds in the world, brought back from the brink of extinction through intensive conservation. Its white plumage takes on a greyish-rose tint during the breeding season.

children.name: Nipponia nippon
children.description: The crested ibis (Nipponia nippon), also known as the Japanese crested ibis, or Asian crested ibis, is a species of ibis, native to eastern Asia.

children.name: Bostrychia
children.description: Forest ibises of sub-Saharan Africa, mostly dark-plumaged inhabitants of swamp forests and woodlands. The Hadada Ibis is one of the most familiar birds of African gardens, named for its loud, raucous call that echoes across suburban Nairobi.

children.name: Bostrychia hagedash
children.description: The hadada ibis (Bostrychia hagedash) or hadeda () is an ibis native to Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Bostrychia carunculata
children.description: The wattled ibis (Bostrychia carunculata) is a species of bird in the family Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Bostrychia olivacea
children.description: The olive ibis (Bostrychia olivacea) is a species of ibis native to dense tropical forests in central Africa.

children.name: Theristicus
children.description: Three or four species of boldly patterned South American ibises with pale bellies and dark wings, found in open grasslands, savannas, and wetlands from the lowlands to the high Andes.

children.name: Theristicus caerulescens
children.description: thumb|Theristicus caerulescens The plumbeous ibis (Theristicus caerulescens), also formerly called the blue ibis, is a large distinctive ibis species endemic to parts of central South America.

children.name: Theristicus oculatus
children.description: A grey ibis of the Andes and Patagonia, with a distinctive dark face and pale eye. It is common in the high-altitude grasslands of Bolivia, Peru, Chile, and Argentina, probing for insects and worms in soft soil.

children.name: Theristicus branickii
children.description: | range_map = Theristicus branickii map.svg.

children.name: Cercibis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Sharp-tailed Ibis, a large, long-legged ibis of South American tropical wetlands named for its exceptionally long, stiff tail feathers.

children.name: Mesembrinibis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Green Ibis, a stocky, dark forest ibis of Central and South America with a distinctive greenish gloss to its plumage.

children.name: Mesembrinibis cayennensis
children.description: The green ibis (Mesembrinibis cayennensis), also known as the Cayenne ibis, is a wading bird in the ibis family Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Phimosus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Bare-faced Ibis, a small, dark ibis with a distinctive bare red face and bill, widespread across South American wetlands.

children.name: Eudocimus
children.description: Two brilliantly coloured American ibises — one white, one scarlet — both with the same elegant body shape and long, slender decurved bill. The Scarlet Ibis is the national bird of Trinidad and Tobago and one of the most vividly coloured birds in the world.

children.name: Eudocimus albus
children.description: The American white ibis is a species of bird in the ibis family, Threskiornithidae. It is found from the southern half of the US East Coast, along the Gulf Coast states and south through most of the Caribbean coastal regions of Central America. This particular ibis species is a medium-sized wading bird, possessing an overall white plumage with black wing-tips, and having the typical downward-curving bill of the ibises, though of a bright red-orange color, the same hue as its long legs.

children.name: Eudocimus ruber
children.description: The scarlet ibis, sometimes called red ibis (Eudocimus ruber), is a species of ibis in the bird family Threskiornithidae.

children.name: Lophotibis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Madagascar Crested Ibis — the only ibis endemic to Madagascar and one of the most beautiful, with a spectacular iridescent crest and wing pattern.

children.name: Lophotibis cristata
children.description: The Madagascar ibis (Lophotibis cristata), also known as the Madagascar crested ibis, white-winged ibis or crested wood ibis, is a medium-sized (approximately 50 cm long), brown-plumaged ibis.

children.name: Ciconia
children.description: Large soaring birds of open farmland and wetlands. The White Stork nested on Swedish farmsteads for centuries before disappearing in the 20th century due to drainage of wet meadows; an active reintroduction programme centred on Skåne has re-established a breeding population. The Black Stork is a shy forest bird, a rare but increasing breeder.

children.name: Ciconia ciconia
children.description: The white stork is a large bird in the stork family, Ciconiidae. Its plumage is mainly white, with black on the bird's wings. Adults have long red legs and long pointed red beaks, and measure on average 100–115 cm (39–45 in) from beak tip to end of tail, with a 155–215 cm (61–85 in) wingspan.

children.name: Ciconia nigra
children.description: The black stork is a large bird in the stork family Ciconiidae. It was first described by Carl Linnaeus in the 10th edition of his Systema Naturae. Measuring on average 95 to 100 cm from beak tip to end of tail with a 145-to-155 cm (57-to-61 in) wingspan, the adult black stork has mainly black plumage, with white underparts, long red legs and a long pointed red beak.

children.name: Ciconia episcopus
children.description: The Asian woolly-necked stork or Asian woollyneck (Ciconia episcopus) is a species of large wading bird in the stork family Ciconiidae.

children.name: Ciconia maguari
children.description: The maguari stork (Ciconia maguari) is a large species of stork that inhabits seasonal wetlands over much of South America, and is very similar in appearance to the white stork; albeit slightly larger.

children.name: Ciconia boyciana
children.description: The Oriental stork is a large, white bird with black-feathered wings in the stork family Ciconiidae.

children.name: Anastomus
children.description: Openbill storks — named for the distinctive gap (anastomosis) between the upper and lower mandibles, an adaptation for feeding on hard-shelled snails and molluscs. The curved bill tips meet only at the front, creating a pincer-like grip for extracting snails from their shells. These medium-sized storks are highly gregarious, nesting in large colonies often mixed with other waterbirds.

children.name: Anastomus oscitans
children.description: The Asian openbill or Asian openbill stork (Anastomus oscitans) is a large wading bird in the stork family Ciconiidae.

children.name: Anastomus lamelligerus
children.description: The African openbill (Anastomus lamelligerus) is a species of stork from the family Ciconiidae.

children.name: Mycteria
children.description: Wood storks and ibises — medium-to-large storks with a distinctive down-curved bill used for tactile foraging in shallow water. They feed by sweeping the bill open in murky water; when it contacts prey, the bill snaps shut in 25 milliseconds — one of the fastest reflexes in the animal kingdom. Highly colonial, often nesting alongside herons, ibises, and cormorants.

children.name: Mycteria americana
children.description: The wood stork (Mycteria americana) is a large wading bird in the family Ciconiidae (storks).

children.name: Mycteria leucocephala
children.description: The painted stork (Mycteria leucocephala) is a large wader in the stork family.

children.name: Mycteria cinerea
children.description: The milky stork (Mycteria cinerea) is a stork species inhabiting predominantly mangroves in Southeast Asia.

children.name: Ephippiorhynchus
children.description: Jabirus and saddle-billed storks — very large, long-legged storks with strikingly patterned plumage and brightly coloured bills with a characteristic saddle-like shield at the base. They are among the tallest flying birds in their respective ranges. Unlike most storks, they are not highly gregarious, nesting as solitary pairs and defending large territories. Males and females have different-coloured irises — a rare trait in birds.

children.name: Jabiru
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the jabiru of the Americas — one of the largest flying birds in the Americas, with a wingspan of up to 2.8 m. Its name comes from the Tupi-Guaraní word for 'swollen neck', referring to its inflatable throat pouch used in courtship displays.

children.name: Leptoptilos
children.description: Adjutant storks and marabou — enormous, bare-headed storks that are among the largest flying birds in their respective ranges. Named 'adjutants' after their stiff, marching gait resembling a military officer. They are primarily scavengers, feeding on carrion, garbage, and carcasses, playing a vital sanitation role in South Asian cities. The marabou of Africa has the largest wingspan of any stork, reaching 3.2 m, yet it is one of the lightest storks thanks to its extremely light, hollow bones.

children.name: Leptoptilos crumenifer
children.description: The marabou stork (Leptoptilos crumenifer) is a large wading bird in the stork family Ciconiidae native to sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Leptoptilos dubius
children.description: The greater adjutant (Leptoptilos dubius) is a member of the stork family, Ciconiidae.

children.name: Leptoptilos javanicus
children.description: The lesser adjutant (Leptoptilos javanicus) is a large wading bird in the stork family Ciconiidae.

children.name: Pelecanus
children.description: Pelicans — unmistakable waterbirds with a massive throat pouch (gular sac) used to scoop fish from the water. The pouch can hold up to 13 litres and is drained before swallowing. Despite their heavy appearance, pelicans are graceful in flight, soaring in formation with slow, powerful wingbeats. They have the largest wingspans of any freshwater bird, reaching 3.5 metres.

children.name: Pelecanus onocrotalus
children.description: The great white pelican (Pelecanus onocrotalus), also known as the eastern white pelican (in contrast to the western pelican of the Americas), rosy pelican or simply white pelican, is a bird in the pelican family.

children.name: Pelecanus crispus
children.description: , Greece]] The Dalmatian pelican (Pelecanus crispus), also known as the curly-headed pelican, is the largest member of the pelican family and among the heaviest flying birds in the world.

children.name: Pelecanus conspicillatus
children.description: The Australian pelican (Pelecanus conspicillatus) is a large waterbird in the family Pelecanidae, widespread on the inland and coastal waters of Australia and New Guinea, also in Fiji, parts of Indonesia and as a vagrant in New Zealand.

children.name: Pelecanus occidentalis
children.description: The brown pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) is a bird of the pelican family, Pelecanidae, one of three species found in the Americas and one of two that feed by diving into water.

children.name: Pelecanus thagus
children.description: The Peruvian pelican (Pelecanus thagus) is a member of the pelican family.

children.name: Pelecanus erythrorhynchos
children.description: The American white pelican (Pelecanus erythrorhynchos) is a large aquatic soaring bird from the order Pelecaniformes.
